name: SparkFun

claims.claim_text: By around 2010 SparkFun was reported to be turning over more than $10 million a year selling open source hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: spark fund, I think are pulling in over $10 million a year now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Roughly a dozen companies at that point had passed the million-dollar annual revenue mark selling open source hobby kits, showing the segment supported more than one viable firm.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's about a dozen companies that have broken this million dollar mark, just selling, you know, open source hobby kits.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Adafruit at the same time was running near a million dollars a year as a two-person operation out of rented space, a far smaller footprint than SparkFun's.
claims.quote_verbatim: art of fruits, almost a million dollars a year now. Wow. Just, just a two person business out of the, you know, out of a rented shopping somewhere.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: A structural hazard of publishing open source hardware is that a larger house like SparkFun or Adafruit can manufacture the same kit at volume and displace the original designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: It does because art of fruit or, or spark fun could come out and manufacture your kit and put you out of business overnight.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: SparkFun's Free Day promotion gave away $100,000 of product in each of two consecutive years, and in the second year a quiz gate was added before the shopping cart.
claims.quote_verbatim: For both years, they've given away $100,000. This year was a little different. They actually made you answer a quiz before you could just go to the shopping cart.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Ben & Jeri Show

claims.claim_text: The giveaway functioned as marketing spend whose return was essentially untrackable: the same $100,000 bought traffic that conventional advertising would not have generated at that price.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, $100,000 in advertising probably did nothing for the amount of people that tried to get to their site.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Ben & Jeri Show

claims.claim_text: SparkFun ran customer forums as a support and community asset rather than as an advertising channel, which is what made customers willing to use them.
claims.quote_verbatim: SparkFun has forums. And I'm not active on them, but I have used them to get information before. And I think that they realize that if you can build a community around your products, but it doesn't feel like advertising, then I think it can work pretty well.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Comical Keyzer Comes a-Callin'

claims.claim_text: SparkFun published Eagle footprints with staggered header pads, a mechanical trick that friction-holds a pin header in the board so it does not fall out during soldering.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, SparkFun released some Eagle footprints for headers that are staggered, and you know why they do that? It's so that if you stick the headers into the board, they don't fall out whenever you try to solder them.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: SparkFun was estimated at $10-15 million annual revenue, implying a company value around $20-30 million using a rough two-times-revenue multiple.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're a $10 million, what, $10, $15 million a year business. So, you know, the company's probably worth, you know, $20, $30 million at least or something like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shonky Stiver Stultiloquence

claims.claim_text: The predicted end state of the open hardware retail sector was consolidation, with the larger firms acquiring each other once they reached sufficient scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: these companies like your Artifruits and your SparkFun, once they get big enough, they'll start gobbling each other up as well
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shonky Stiver Stultiloquence

claims.claim_text: SparkFun's catalog practice was to link customers to working code libraries for each sensor it stocked, including libraries the company had not authored itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I know like SparkFun is good about pointing you towards code libraries for the sensors and things that they sell, even if they didn't write the code.
claims.speaker: Jeff Rowberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: SparkFun held a company-wide culture meeting once a year in which employees collectively defined what working there should be like.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually have a culture meeting once a year, a company-wide meeting where we all get together and discuss, you know, what we want it to be like working at SparkFun.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: New product ideas came through a dedicated scout who surfaced candidate parts and pitched them to the whole engineering group, which then selected which ones to develop.
claims.quote_verbatim: Pierce is really good at finding possible new products and he presents them to all us and we all talk about them and pick the cool stuff and run with it.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Engineers at SparkFun were allowed to propose products drawn from their own interests rather than only working from a centrally assigned roadmap.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a lot of latitude that you're allowed to kind of present things that you yourself are interested in that you think might be a product
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Because its customer base ranged from beginners to NASA engineers, SparkFun could not predict demand in advance and instead used the storefront itself as the test, relying on being small enough to try a product and observe.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've got everything from beginners to like people on NASA and we're not always quite sure what we'll sell if we put it on the storefront and we're, we're small and agile enough that we'll actually try it and see, see what happens
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Product retention decisions were only loosely tied to sales metrics; a part judged interesting enough would be kept in the catalog even while losing money.
claims.quote_verbatim: If something's cool, we will keep it on the site and let it just fail financially for, yeah.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Chinese cloners could reproduce a SparkFun kit within days of release, forcing the company onto a permanent treadmill of introducing new designs to stay ahead.
claims.quote_verbatim: They, they are in a very, very difficult position and it is a constant uphill fight for them. I mean, they've got to stay on the edge or other people catch up.
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: SparkFun's defense against clones of its open source designs was not the designs themselves but brand, service and value-added support, sustaining a business estimated at $15-20 million turnover.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're talking about a 15, $20 million turnover business or something. And they're going great guns and they survive because of their brand and because people like them and because of their value added services.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Margins in the open hardware kit and breakout board trade were thin, constraining how much engineering and support any one product could carry.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mean, yeah, SparkFun and Adafruit are fantastic. And margins are small.
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: SparkFun acted as a contract manufacturer for outside products, having built and shipped 11,000 units of the Makey Makey on behalf of its creators.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they shipped SparkFun on behalf of Makey Makey, made this product and shipped 11,000 units.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A small hardware firm that had already done its own fabrication, picking, packing and order shipping chose to outsource all of it to SparkFun rather than repeat that work in house.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been through the process of fabricating my own hardware before. I've been through the process of, you know, picking and packing and shipping orders. Why don't we get some other bastard to do this? And we approached SparkFun
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: The commercial value of a SparkFun manufacturing deal was that the product entered SparkFun's own distributor network, reported at around 500 distributors, not just its retail site.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, but not just SparkFun, but also their 500 distributors who distribute for SparkFun.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Seeed Studio and Adafruit were evaluated as alternative manufacturing and distribution partners before SparkFun was selected, indicating a small comparison set at that scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I ran the numbers. I looked at Seed Studio. I looked at Adafruit.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: SparkFun and Adafruit each staffed whole teams whose output was free tutorial content on their learn sites, treating documentation as a funded product line rather than a side task.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're employing, like, not just one person, but teams of people building free content
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: SparkFun remained a private company with essentially all equity held by a single owner, which limited any outside acquisition path.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a private company owned by 99.99% by one guy.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: SparkFun tried to import 2,000 China-made SparkFun-branded multimeters selling at about $15 retail against an estimated $5 landed cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: tried to import 2000 multimeters, little $15 ones, probably cost them five bucks a pop, right? Straight out of China. Like they're spark fun branded
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: The Fluke seizure rested on trade dress rather than trademark, an untested claim that SparkFun might have beaten in court had it been able to fund the fight.
claims.quote_verbatim: trade dress is not like a trademark. It's not like you've copied their logo and it's absolutely obvious and you're going to lose that court case. It's probably, if SparkFun had enough money, they could probably challenge this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: Fluke's public statement was framed so that SparkFun would give the released meters away rather than sell them, converting a legal outcome into a reputational obligation.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fluke, uh, press release was worded in a, you know, not so subtle way that sort of hinted that spark fun should give these away.
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: By the mid-2010s SparkFun's revenue was put at $30 million or more, up from the roughly $10 million figure circulating a few years earlier.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because SparkFun are a hundred million dollar company. Yeah. No. Are they? They're a $30 million company at least.
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: SparkFun ran a data-collection service that hardware could push readings to over a simple URL, which then stored and re-served the stream in a machine-readable format for third-party graphing front ends.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the SparkFun thing pings that URL and then tracks the data and then spits it out in a friendly format.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Warming Up To IoT - Tendentious Thermal Tools

claims.claim_text: SparkFun's cloud data service was positioned as an enabler for its own hardware sales to hobbyists rather than as a competitor to general-purpose IoT platforms like Amazon's.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the Sparkfund service is very much geared towards hobbyists, and it's more of an enabling tool for Sparkfund hardware.
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: The SparkFun data service was released as open source, so a user could run the same server on a local machine or a private VPS instead of depending on SparkFun's hosted instance.
claims.quote_verbatim: the other thing about the SparkFun service is that it's completely open source. So, you can get your own SparkFun server running on a local machine or you could spin up your own VPS.
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: The tutorial-first commerce model works by leading with a project the customer wants to complete and making the parts merely available alongside it, rather than pushing the sale.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then, oh, along the way, like, yeah, if you're going to buy this stuff, of course we have it available. But it's not like, you must buy this. It's just, here it is.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: The core economics of the SparkFun-style business is producing breakout boards cheaply enough that a small company can sustain a broad catalog.
claims.quote_verbatim: like it's making breakout boards effectively. And you can do that in a cost effective way
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: SparkFun was the larger of the two open hardware retailers when Adafruit was still small, and the relative sizes later reversed.
claims.quote_verbatim: When I was starting this originally, you know, SparkFun, uh, was kind of the big guys out there, at least in this world. I think Adafruit at the time was a little bit smaller.
claims.speaker: Ken Burns
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: SparkFun manufactured the Teensy under contract for its designer, while Adafruit acted as a reseller of the finished boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: because Art of Fruit were selling the teensy, which is, which SparkFun make on behalf of the guy who designed it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: The Teensy's designer stopped building the boards himself and handed production to SparkFun, an example of a one-person hardware product outsourcing manufacturing to a larger open hardware firm.
claims.quote_verbatim: he used to make it himself, but then he decided, no, I don't want to make it myself anymore. So he got SparkFun to make it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: SparkFun revoked Adafruit's right to resell the Teensy, citing a code of conduct violation rather than any commercial or technical dispute over the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: And SparkFun have just announced, yeah, that they're not letting Art of Fruit resell it anymore because of codes of conduct violation.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: The dispute escalated to a full cutoff in which Adafruit was barred from reselling any SparkFun product, severing a long-standing cross-distribution relationship between the two firms.
claims.quote_verbatim: And as a result, Art of Fruit are no longer allowed to sell SparkFun stuff.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: The Teensy is only partly open: its libraries are open source but the board ships a proprietary bootloader the designer was contractually unable to release.
claims.quote_verbatim: All of the libraries and stuff are, but it uses a proprietary NDA bootloader, which Paul wanted to make it open source, but he couldn't.
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: The bootloader could not be opened because the designer had signed a non-disclosure agreement with the silicon vendor whose microcontroller the board uses.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because he signed an NDA with NXP, I think it is, who make the chip that's on the teensy.
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate
